blocks.text: The Begena (በገና) is classed among the stringed musical instruments (chordophones). It is more than five thousand eight hundred years old, and can be called the father of the stringed instruments. It stands apart in the power with which it draws a person into deep contemplation (መመስጥ), in its calmness, in the fact that it is sung with on its own, in its poetic words (ሥነ ቃል) and in similar values.

It serves both in heaven and on earth, and is used for spiritual service only. The making of each of its parts, their names and what they stand for are all spiritual, and it is a spiritual instrument that leads those who play it toward spiritual life. What follows are the meanings of “Begena” that various fathers have set down.

sections.heading: The grammatical meaning (Aleqa Kidanewold Kifle, አለቃ ኪዳነ ወልድ ክፍሌ)

blocks.text: Aleqa Kidanewold explained the word in two ways, relating it to “when it tightens and when it loosens”:
When it loosens: it means to shake or pluck (ነዘረ), to strike (መታ), to play (ደረደረ).
When it tightens: it means to burn (ነደደ), to become angry (ተቆጣ), and the like.
In Hebrew the Begena is called “Nagen” (ናጌን). He also explained that, taken literally, Begena means “psalm” (መዝሙር). The evidence for this is the Holy Scripture:
“ግነዩ ለእግዚአብሔር በመሰንቆ ወበመዝሙር ዘአስርቱ አውታሪሁ”
“Praise the Lord with the mesenqo (መሰንቆ), and sing to him with the Begena that has ten strings.” Psalm 32/33:2
“አፀምአ ምሳሌ በእዝንየ፤ ወእከስት በመዝሙር ነገርየ”
“I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will express my matter on the Begena.” Psalm 48/49:4–5
Further references given in the original: Psalm 56/57:8, 70/71:22, 91/92:3, 97/98:5, 107/108:2, 143/144:9 and 149/150:3.
The Ge’ez Bible refers to the Begena everywhere as “mezmur” (መዝሙር, psalm). In the verses above, the word “ወበመዝሙር” is used to point to the Begena.

Kesate Birhan Tessema (ከሳቴ ብርሃን ተሰማ) defined it as follows. Begena: he made a Begena with ten strings (sinews, ጅማት), tuned it, played it, sounding its notes clearly and plucking them. They say he “begenu” (በገነ) the Begena. Begenyña (በገነኛ): one who strikes the Begena, one who knows the Begena; a player (ደርዳሪ).

Begenu (በገኑ) means to dry, to scorch, to set alight. “Begena” is a name that comes from this. The main reason this meaning is found is that the whole body of the Begena is made from dry things: dry wood, dry skin and dry sinew. So it is explained that it was called Begena.
Begena, when split into “be” (በ) and “gena” (ገና): it is an instrument of thanksgiving that is played at the feast or season of Gena (Christmas), so it is explained that it was called Begena.
To “begenu” the Begena (በገናን በገኑ) means to play it (ደረደረ). So Begena means playing, praise, psalm. The evidence for this is again the Bible:
“O Lord my God, I will praise you on the Begena.” Psalm 42/43:4
“Play the Begena for the Lord.” Psalm 46:6
“Praise the Lord with the mesenqo; sing to him with the Begena that has ten strings.” Psalm 32/33:2

From both sides (the grammatical and the word-origin), and starting from where the meanings overlap, the meaning that comes closest, in its inner sense, to the spiritual and social service of the Begena is “begenu” = to play, to strike. David, the Begena player, when he explains the Begena in his psalms, describes it as psalm, praise and playing (ድርደራ).

The Begena is first mentioned in the Bible in Genesis 4:22, where Jubal (ዮባል, Yobal), son of Lamech, is named as the father of those who hold the Begena and the trumpet (መለከት). This account also shows that there were others who held the Begena and the trumpet, and that Jubal was their chief. From that time the Begena was known as an instrument of melody for giving thanks to God and, like the other instruments of the temple, it was used in service under chiefs chosen from among the Levites. In all, the Begena is mentioned in the Bible, from Genesis to the Revelation of John, more than 50 times.

sections.heading: The historical beginning of the Begena

blocks.text: It is hard to say exactly when and how the Begena began. But since the Bible is the source of the arts, the Bible tells us that the first instrument of praise or melody it shows is the Begena. The first to play the Begena were the children of Jubal (Iyubel, ኢዩቤል), son of Lamech (Genesis 4:22–24). The Andimta commentary (አንድምታ ትርጓሜ) of Memher Musie Hailu (መምህር ሙሴ ኃይሉ) explains the account above more fully:

“The first to play the Begena were the children of Jubal (Iyubel), son of Lamech. This is how it was. Their grandfather Lamech, who was blind, was walking in the wilderness. Cain was a wanderer and had hidden himself alone at the edge of the place. [Lamech] heard a rustling, and said to the guide (ረዳዕ) who led him on the road: ‘…I hear the leaves rustling. It seems wild beasts have come upon us. Hand me a stone.’ After that he took the stone and threw it in the direction he had heard, and it struck Cain on the forehead and killed him. When they came near and saw that it was Cain, he wept bitterly. After this, Lamech’s two wives told their children what Lamech had told them about his remorse. This account was passed down through the generations until it reached the grandchildren of Lamech (the children of Jubal). Thinking of the terrible story of killing among their fathers, starting from Abel, and grieving over it, they made Begenas from dry materials and, singing softly in sorrow, they expressed their grief.”
So the Begena began to be played in the ninth generation from Adam. The line of generations is this:
Adam (አዳም) begot Cain (ቃኤል, Qa’el).
Cain begot Henoch (ሄኖሕ, Henoh).
Henoch begot Gaidad (ጋይዳድ, Gaydad).
Gaidad begot Me’el (ሜኤል).
Me’el begot Matusa’el (ማቱሣኤል).
Matusa’el begot Lamech (ላሜሕ).
Lamech begot Jubal (ዮባል).
Jubal was the father of those who play the Begena. (Their names are not clearly stated in the Bible.)
It was through these fathers, the grandchildren of Lamech who were of the ninth generation from Adam, that the Begena was prepared…

sections.heading: Let us know Tewahedo: the division of the Ten Commandments

blocks.text: The Christian law is the law of love. After saying that whoever loves another has fulfilled the law, Saint Paul names some of the Ten Commandments and states plainly that love is the fulfilment of all the law (Romans 13:8–10). Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ also taught us that love is divided into two (Matthew 22:34–41):
Love of God (ፍቅረ እግዚአብሔር, Fikre Egziabher): loving God.
Love of neighbour (ፍቅረ ቢጽ, Fikre Bits): loving one’s brother.
Because our Lord also said that the Law and the Prophets are summed up in these two commandments, we divide the Ten Commandments into two on this basis.
The first to the third commandments:
You shall have no other gods before me.
You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.
Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
The fourth to the tenth commandments:
Honour your father and your mother.
You shall not kill.
You shall not commit adultery.
You shall not steal.
You shall not bear false witness.
You shall not covet your neighbour’s house.
Love your neighbour as yourself.

sections.heading: The parts of the Begena and what they stand for (1)

blocks.text: How it is made. The Begena is made from wood and animal products (skin, gut, horn). Its height reaches from 90 to 140 cm. The strings are twisted from cattle (ox) gut.
What it stands for: a symbol of the authority of God (ስልጣነ እግዚአብሔር, Siltane Egziabher).
What it stands for: a symbol of the Cross, on which God showed his perfect love for humankind.
What it stands for: the Meqanya is likened to the Holy Spirit (መንፈስ ቅዱስ, Menfes Qidus), because it is He who protects the life of the faithful by giving the laws.
Alternatively: the Meqanya are likened to the saints, the righteous and the martyrs who overcame this world and joined the body of the victorious Church in heaven.
Alternatively: a symbol of the angels.

sections.heading: ቀኝ ምሰሶ (Qegn Miseso), the right pillar

blocks.text: What it stands for: a symbol of the love of God (ፍቅረ እግዚአብሔር, Fikre Egziabher). Alternatively: of the Old Testament (ብሉይ ኪዳን, Bluy Kidan). Alternatively: of Megabe Bluy (መጋቤ ብሉይ), Saint Michael (ቅዱስ ሚካኤል, Qidus Mikael).

sections.heading: ግራ ምሰሶ (Gra Miseso), the left pillar

blocks.text: What it stands for: a symbol of the love of one’s neighbour, that is, of people (ፍቅረ ቢጽ, Fikre Bits). Alternatively: of the New Testament (ሐዲስ ኪዳን, Hadis Kidan). Alternatively: of Megabe Hadis (መጋቤ ሐዲስ), Saint Gabriel (ቅዱስ ገብርኤል, Qidus Gebre’el).
What it stands for: a symbol of the Ten Commandments (አሥርቱ ትዕዛዛት, Asirtu Te’zazat) (Exodus 20:1–17). The ten strings also stand for:

The ten senses. The outer five: the eye, the nose, the ear, the tongue and the palm. The inner five: ዓይነ ልቦና (Ayne Libona), አንፈ ልቦና (Anfe Libona), እዝነ ልቦና (Izne Libona), አፈ ልቦና (Afe Libona) and እደ ልቦና (Ede Libona), literally the eye, nose, ear, mouth and hand of the heart.
The three melodic modes of Saint Yared (ቅዱስ ያሬድ): ግእዝ (Ge’ez), for the Father; ዕዝል (Ezl), for the Son; and አራራይ (Araray), for the Holy Spirit.
The ten headings of Saint David’s Psalms, under which he divided the 150 psalms into ten.

The ten ranks of the saints: ንጽሐ ሥጋ (Nitsehe Sega, purity of body), ንጽሐ ነፍስ (Nitsehe Nefs, purity of soul) and ንጽሐ ልቦና (Nitsehe Libona, purity of heart), arranged in three groups called ወጣንያን (Wetanyan), ማዕከላውያን (Ma’ekelawiyan) and ፍጹማን (Fitsuman).

sections.heading: ገበቴ (Gebete), the sound box · የድምጽ ሳጥን (Yedimts Satin)

blocks.text: What it stands for: a symbol of Our Lady, the Holy Virgin Mary (እመቤታችን ድንግል ማርያም, Emebetachin Dingil Mariyam). Just as the sound of the Begena comes from the sound box (the Gebete), from Our Lady came the incarnate Word (አካላዊ ቃል, Akalawi Qal), the Son, our Lord, Saviour and God, Jesus Christ.
What it stands for: a symbol of Mount Sinai (ደብረ ሲና, Debre Sina).

It is made from wood and skin and is found at the lower part of the Begena. It is used to stretch the strings together with the Qenber (the strings are stretched between the two). The ten strings join these two parts, the Qenber and the Mewetteriya.

The Mewetteriya is likened to the dwelling place of people (the earth). This means that it is a symbol of people entering the kingdom of heaven from the earth by the ladder of the commandments of God (ትዕዛዛተ እግዚእ, Te’zazate Egzi’).
Alternatively: it stands for the descendants of Adam on earth (humankind).

What it stands for: the Enzira are likened to Christians who are in spiritual struggle (ተጋድሎ, Tegadlo). Just as the Enzira sit on the ten strings, Christians struggle to enrich their spiritual life in their life in the world, taking as their guide the commandments of God, which the ten strings stand for.

A striker made of horn. It is used to strike the strings so that they give sound. The Dehntsa is likened to Christ. Just as the Dehntsa goes back and forth, striking the ten strings, so Jesus Christ, Saviour of the world, confirmed in the New Testament the ten commandments that he gave in the Old Testament.

sections.heading: The cross-shaped mark on the back of the Gebete · የመስቀል ምልክት (Yemeskel Milikit)

blocks.text: The cross-shaped mark on the back of the sound box (the Gebete) is the sign of how Saint David was saved from the spear of Saul. In the New Testament the Cross is also our sign of being saved from the arrows of the devil, and so this mark is made.

The Begena is played with the fingers of the left hand (this is the tradition). The right hand supports the pillar on the chest side. It is explained that the left hand stirs the right half of the brain, the “station of feeling” that develops artistic thinking.
The Begena is played in two ways:
ድርደራ (Dirdera): the fingers rest on each string in turn and play it.
መግረፍ (Megref): the Dehntsa is used to strike all ten strings.

sections.heading: 5.2 The names of the fingers and where they rest

blocks.text: Strings 1, 4, 6, 8 and 10 give the main notes. The other five strings are resting and accompanying strings (ማረፊያ, Marefiya, and ማጀቢያ, Majebiya).
In the original, a drawing here shows the ten strings, each labelled with its number.
A qinyit (ቅኝት) is a formula that holds the basic notes of a melodic style. There is no melody without a qinyit.

In Ethiopia the four main qinyitoch are ትዝታ (Tizita), ባቲ (Bati), አንቺ ሆዬ ለኔ (Anchi Hoye Lene) and አምባሰል (Ambassel). These are qinyitoch of five notes (pentatonic), and they take their names from famous folk melodies and from place names. In addition to these, the ሰላምታ (Selamta) qinyit is used in Begena melodies.

sections.heading: 6.2 The five main notes of the Begena [in C]

blocks.text: In the Selamta qinyit:
The Tizita qinyit differs from Selamta in that the first string (F) is lowered to E. In Anchi Hoye Lene, the 6th and 10th strings are lowered by a semitone. [ሲ]

sections.heading: 6.3 Which qinyit should we begin with?

blocks.text: Begena teachers recommend starting with the Selamta qinyit, because it is the usual one in Begena melodies, and the student becomes familiar with the melody through songs like “Selam Leki” (ሰላም ለኪ).
All of the qinyitoch are obtained from the seven European notes (diatonic: C D E F G A B) by taking out two notes and lowering some of the others by a semitone.

rows: The melody the name was taken from
C D F G A C
Take out the 3rd and the 7th notes.
“Selam Leki” (ሰላም ለኪ), that is “Selam Le Mariyam” (ሰላም ለማርያም)
C D E G A C
Take out the 4th and the 7th notes. It differs from Selamta by one note only (F becomes E).
C D E♭ G A♭ C
Lower the 3rd and 5th notes of Wanen by a semitone (E to E♭, A to A♭).
“Anchi Hoye” (አንቺ ሆዬ), “Sile Chernetih” (ስለ ቸርነትህ) (as given in the original)
C D♭ F G♭ A C
Lower the 2nd and 5th notes of the five notes of Selamta (D and G) by a semitone. On the Begena these are the 6th and 10th strings.
“Sile Chernetih Geta Temesgen” (ስለ ቸርነትህ ጌታ ተመስገን)
C D♭ F G A♭ C
Lower the 2nd and 5th notes of the five notes (D and A) by a semitone.
The area of Wollo Ambassel (የወሎ አምባሰል)
C E F G B C
Take out the 2nd and the 6th of the seven notes. Compared with Selamta, D becomes E and A becomes B (a whole tone higher).
The area of Wollo Bati (የወሎ ባቲ)
C E♭ F G B♭ C
Lower the 2nd and 5th notes of Bati major by a semitone (E to E♭, B to B♭).

blocks.text: All the qinyitoch need care and ear training for a student to tell them apart. In particular, Selamta and Wanen differ by only one note, so they must be listened to well.
Compared with Selamta, the “Sile Chernetih” qinyit differs only in the 6th and 10th strings. So a Begena tuned to Selamta can be changed into this qinyit by lowering those two strings by a semitone.

There are hymns sung for each qinyit, and the student is made to remember the qinyit by linking it with its hymn. For example: Selamta, “Hode Limed” (ሆዴ ልመድ), “Be-Gete Semani” (በጌቴ ሰማኒ), “Bemeskel Teseqilo” (በመስቀል ተሰቅሎ); Wanen, “Rigbena Wanen” (ርግብና ዋኔን); Anchi Hoye, “Sile Chernetih” (ስለ ቸርነትህ).

In Ethiopian music, Ambassel and Bati are linked with secular songs. For that reason they are placed in the book as additional qinyitoch for the Begena. A separate spiritual melody is sung on the Begena in these qinyitoch.
Order of learning: first Selamta, then Wanen, then Anchi Hoye Lene (Sile Chernetih), and after that Ambassel, Nu’us Wanen, Bati and Bati minor.
